challenges.name: grounding-and-uncertainty
challenges.title: Grounding and "I'm not sure"
challenges.description: Two statements on the billing FAQ bot that promised a 30-day refund: what a stronger instruction can and cannot do, and how a citation check treats an answer.

questions.question:
Prompt log, request fq_3c90 (the full prompt):
You are the CodeDev billing assistant. Answer questions about prices, points and refunds.
IMPORTANT: Never make up information. Do not hallucinate.

Question: Can I get a refund for a premium course I bought last week?

Answer: Yes! Premium courses can be refunded within 30 days of purchase, no questions asked.
Log: model=chat-small-2025-01 temperature=0.3 docs_attached=0 finish_reason=stop
Refund policy page: refundable within 7 days of purchase if less than 20% of the lessons are finished.

Statement: "Adding one more line - "Only answer if you are 100% sure" - would stop answers like this one, because the model would then check how sure it is before it answers."
questions.explanation: False. The prompt contains no refund policy (docs_attached=0), so the model has no fact to answer from, and it has no reliable signal that tells it a sentence is invented: "30 days" and "7 days" come out of the same next-token process. Another instruction adds no information and its effect is unmeasured; it may even make the bot refuse questions it could answer. What fixes this answer is grounding - the refund-policy section in the prompt, a rule to answer only from it with a citation, an allowed "I'm not sure" - checked with eval cases. The misconception is that a model can be instructed into knowing what it does not know.

True. The answer is not an "I'm not sure" reply and it does contain a citation, so the check reaches the loop: refund-policy is not one of the sections that were sent (points-pricing, certificates), so it returns { kind: "reject" } with the reason "cites refund-policy, which was not in the prompt". A rejected answer is never shown; the user gets the unsure message with a next step, and the rejection is logged. The misconception is that any citation proves grounding: a model can produce a plausible id just as it produces a plausible fact, so the id must be compared with what was actually sent.
